issues.legal_issue: A court must give an accused a reasonable opportunity to be heard before disposing of an application seeking relief in a criminal appeal.
material_facts: The accused filed an application seeking further examination of witnesses and other relief in the High Court.
The application was not listed or heard in court and was disposed of in the judge’s chambers without hearing the accused’s counsel.
issues.conclusion: The application should have been disposed of after hearing the accused’s counsel; disposing of it without that opportunity was wrong and unjust, and the accused had a just grievance about the procedure.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the requirement of a reasonable opportunity to be heard when disposing of an application under section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The accused pursued a criminal appeal from a conviction.
predicates.application_disposed_without_hearing: The court disposed of the accused’s application without hearing the accused or counsel in court.
predicates.application_disposal_was_unjust: The court disposed of the application unjustly by denying the accused a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a criminal conviction and the court disposes of the accused’s application without a hearing, the disposition is unjust.

issues.legal_issue: A forgery conviction cannot safely rest on an approver’s unreliable testimony when there is no material corroboration connecting the accused to the crime.
material_facts: The prosecution’s account of the alleged forgery rested principally on an approver whose testimony the Court found unimpressive and hardly trustworthy.
The approver’s claims about the pattas and signatures were not supported by reliable evidence connecting the accused to the alleged forgery.
The pattas bore the accused’s own signatures, and the evidence did not establish that he forged another person’s signatures on them.
The evidence did not establish that the consideration was below market value, had been misappropriated, or that a purchaser had been cheated.
Evidence from other witnesses and documents did not provide reliable corroboration of the approver’s allegations.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for forgery of valuable security was wholly unsustainable on the existing evidence and had to be set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 133 of the Indian Evidence Act, an accomplice is a competent witness and a conviction is not illegal merely because it rests on uncorroborated accomplice testimony. That provision must be read with section 114, illustration (b), which states the prudential warning that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless corroborated in material particulars. Ordinarily, corroboration should connect or tend to connect the accused with the crime, though it need not independently suffice to sustain conviction. The court should first assess whether the approver’s testimony is otherwise acceptable. The Court also applied sections 30, 463 and 467 of the Indian Penal Code concerning valuable security and forgery. The judgment cites no earlier cases for these principles.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_forgery_conviction: The accused pursued a criminal appeal against a conviction for forgery.
predicates.approver_testimony_unreliable: The court found the approver’s testimony unimpressive or otherwise unreliable.
predicates.no_material_accused_linking_corroboratio: The prosecution presented no reliable material corroborating the approver in particulars connecting the accused to the alleged crime.
predicates.forgery_conviction_must_be_set_aside: The conviction for forgery cannot stand and must be set aside.

issues.definition: A forgery conviction in a criminal appeal must be set aside when the approver’s testimony is unreliable and no material corroboration connects the accused to the crime.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal-conspiracy conviction cannot be sustained on an uncorroborated and unconvincing approver’s account when the alleged acts said to show a common criminal purpose are not established by acceptable evidence.
material_facts: The only evidence of the alleged conspiracy was the approver’s testimony, which the Court found unconvincing and had not accepted as reliable regarding the alleged forgery.
The approver’s account was uncorroborated, and although he claimed to have prepared many pattas and order sheets, the evidence concerning the documents charged was not trustworthy.
The approver first disclosed the alleged conspiracy to the police after his arrest while expecting assistance from them.
The alleged acts in furtherance of a common criminal purpose were not established by evidence the Court accepted.
issues.conclusion: The charge of conspiracy could not be sustained on the available evidence; the conviction was quashed and the accused acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, conspiracy is commonly proved by inference because direct independent evidence is seldom available; the inference is ordinarily drawn from parties’ acts in pursuit of an apparent common criminal purpose. An accomplice may prove conspiracy, but the Court applied the prudential approach in section 114, illustration (b), of the Indian Evidence Act and found the sole approver’s uncorroborated account insufficient here. The judgment cites no earlier cases for these principles.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conspiracy_convicti: The accused pursued a criminal appeal against a conviction for conspiracy.
predicates.conspiracy_evidence_is_only_approver: The prosecution’s evidence of the alleged conspiracy consisted only of an accomplice who testified as an approver.
predicates.approver_testimony_unconvincing: The court found the approver’s account of the alleged conspiracy unconvincing.
predicates.no_reliable_acts_show_common_criminal_pu: The prosecution presented no reliable evidence of acts by the accused and others in pursuit of an apparent common criminal purpose.
predicates.conspiracy_conviction_cannot_be_sustaine: The conviction for conspiracy cannot stand on the evidence.

issues.definition: A conspiracy conviction cannot stand where the only evidence is an unconvincing approver’s account and no reliable acts establish a common criminal purpose.
